setup.title: Set up your organisation
setup.subtitle: A few short steps to tailor CoreFlow to how you work. You can come back and change everything later.

profile.title: Tell us about your organisation
profile.body: Industry, size and countries help CoreFlow suggest what is relevant to you.

banner.body: A short wizard helps you choose frameworks, turn on the right modules and get the first tasks going.

intro.title: Modules match CoreFlow to your management system
intro.body: Each module covers one area the standards ask for, such as risk, audits or training. Turn on only what you need; you can add more as your system grows.

steps.s1: Start with the modules the setup wizard recommends for your frameworks.
steps.s2: Check the "Needs" hint: some modules build on others.
steps.s3: Turning a module off hides it but keeps its records.

why.body: Standards expect a defined set of processes (the process approach) and risk-based planning. Choosing modules deliberately documents which processes your system includes.

intro.title: The profile describes your context
intro.body: ISO management systems start with understanding the organisation, the interested parties and the scope. The profile is the short version of that context.

steps.s1: Fill in industry, size and the countries you operate in.
steps.s2: Tick the frameworks in scope and add certification targets with dates.
steps.s3: Choose your role under the EU AI Act. "Not sure yet" is fine for now.

why.body: Clauses 4.1 to 4.3 require you to understand your context, the needs of interested parties and the scope of the system. Auditors often start here.

industry.help: In your own words, for example "food production" or "IT consulting".

countries.help: Two-letter codes, separated by commas. Laws and regulators depend on them.

description.help: What you do, for whom and where. A few sentences are enough.

frameworks.help: The frameworks decide which requirements and modules CoreFlow suggests.

aiActRole.help: Providers build AI systems; deployers use them. Many organisations are deployers without knowing it.

targets.help: A target date makes the plan concrete and helps you schedule audits and reviews.

sites.help: List the locations your management system covers. It shapes the scope statement.

intro.title: Speak your organisation's language
intro.body: People follow a system more easily when it uses their words. Change the wording here and CoreFlow uses it everywhere.

steps.s1: Pick the terms you call something else, for example "nonconformity" for deviation.
steps.s2: Fill in the singular and the plural for each language you use.
steps.s3: Save, and check the preview above the list.

why.body: Awareness and communication (clause 7.4) work better in familiar language, and controlled documents (clause 7.5) should use terms consistently.

intro.title: Set up in a few minutes
intro.body: The wizard walks you through the basics of a management system: context, scope, the right modules, roles and the first tasks.

steps.s1: Describe the organisation and choose the frameworks in scope.
steps.s2: Review the recommended modules. Use "Ask why" if something is unclear.
steps.s3: Invite people and start with a few first tasks.

why.body: The scope (clause 4.3), roles and responsibilities (clause 5.3) and planning for risks (clause 6.1) are the foundation every later audit checks.

modulesBasics.title: Frameworks, modules and your management system

s1.heading: One structure, many standards
s1.body: ISO 9001, 27001, 14001, 42001 and 45001 share the same clause structure, from context (4) to improvement (10). Work you do once, such as a management review, can count for several standards.

s2.heading: Frameworks decide the requirements
s2.body: A framework is the standard or regulation you follow. It decides what you must be able to show an auditor, for example a risk assessment or training records.

s3.heading: Modules are where the work happens
s3.body: A module is the part of CoreFlow where you do that work and keep the evidence. Turn on the modules your frameworks need and leave the rest off until you need them.

q1.question: What decides which requirements you must meet?
q1.explanation: The frameworks decide the requirements; modules are where you meet them.

q2.question: What happens to the records when you turn a module off?

options.c: They are kept and come back when you turn it on

q2.explanation: Turning a module off only hides it; the records stay.
